content: 1. For adults, administer the preferred regimen of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid at a dose of 500 mg twice daily (BID) for 10 days. For children, the preferred regimen is amoxicillin-clavulanic acid at 40 mg/kg/day orally, divided into three doses (TID) for 10 days. 2. An alternative regimen involves a single intramuscular (IM) dose of benzathine penicillin G (1,200,000 units for patients weighing ≥27 kg) with or without rifampin at 20 mg/kg/day orally, divided into two doses (BID) for 4 days. 3. For secondary prophylaxis of rheumatic fever: The preferred regimen is benzathine penicillin G (1,200,000 units IM) every 4 weeks for patients weighing ≥27 kg. Alternative regimens include penicillin V potassium at 250 mg orally BID or sulfadiazine at 1 g orally once daily (QD) for patients weighing ≥27 kg. Duration of treatment depends on the presence of residual cardiac disease: If residual cardiac disease is present, continue treatment until the patient is 40 years old or for 10 years, whichever is longer. If no residual cardiac disease is present, continue treatment for 10 years or until the patient is 21 years old, whichever is longer. For rheumatic fever without carditis, continue treatment for 5 years or until the patient is 21 years old, whichever is longer. 4. For patients allergic to penicillin and sulfadiazine, consider using a macrolide or azalide antibiotic. 5. For Streptococcus pyogenes bacteremia: The preferred regimen is penicillin G (4 million units IV every 4 hours) combined with clindamycin (900 mg IV every 8 hours) for at least 14 days. Penicillin is included to cover any group A streptococcus strains resistant to clindamycin. Alternative regimens include erythromycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin, or other β-lactam antibiotics. Note: Macrolide resistance is increasing. Consider intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) in patients with invasive infection and signs of shock. Administer IVIG at 1 g/kg on day 1, followed by 0.5 g/kg on days 2 and 3. If shock is present, provide massive IV fluids (10–20 L/day), albumin if serum levels are <2 g/dL, and debridement of necrotic tissue. 6. For Streptococcus pyogenes cellulitis, treat as Streptococcus pyogenes bacteremia. 7. For epiglottitis in children: Preferred regimens include cefotaxime (50 mg/kg IV every 8 hours) or ceftriaxone (50 mg/kg IV every 24 hours). Alternative regimens include amoxicillin-sulbactam (100–200 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours) or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (8–12 mg/kg BID). Note: Keep a tracheostomy set at the bedside. 8. For burn wound sepsis: The preferred regimen is vancomycin (1 g IV every 12 hours) combined with amikacin (10 mg/kg IV loading dose, then 7.5 mg/kg IV every 12 hours). Piperacillin-tazobactam may be used if piperacillin is unavailable. 9. For necrotizing fasciitis, consult a surgeon for emergent fasciotomy and debridement. Repeat debridements are often necessary. 10. For myositis, surgical debridement is recommended. 11. For acute bacterial keratitis: The preferred regimen is moxifloxacin eye drops (1 drop TID for 7 days). Alternative therapy includes gatifloxacin eye drops (1–2 drops every 2 hours while awake for 2 days, then every 4 hours for 3–7 days). Note: Moxifloxacin is preferred due to its enhanced lipophilicity and penetration into the aqueous humor. 12. For keratitis due to dry cornea, diabetes, or immunosuppression: The preferred regimen is cefazolin (50 mg/mL) combined with gentamicin or tobramycin (14 mg/mL) administered every 15–60 minutes around the clock for 24–72 hours, followed by a slow reduction in frequency. Alternative therapy includes vancomycin (50 mg/mL) combined with ceftazidime (50 mg/mL) administered in the same manner. Note: Therapy should be guided by culture and sensitivity results. 13. For dacryocystitis (lacrimal sac infection): The preferred regimen is moxifloxacin eye drops (1 drop TID for 7 days) or cefazolin (50 mg/mL). 14. For suppurative phlebitis: The preferred regimen is vancomycin (15 mg/kg IV every 12 hours for normal weight). An alternative regimen is daptomycin (6 mg/kg IV every 12 hours). Note: Retrospective studies recommend 2–3 weeks of IV therapy followed by 2 weeks of oral therapy. 15. For infected prosthetic joints: The preferred regimen is penicillin G (2 million units IV every 4 hours) or ceftriaxone (2 g IV every 24 hours) for 4 weeks. Note: Debridement and prosthesis retention with intravenous antibiotics are recommended. 16. For tender parotid swelling (hot parotid): The preferred regimen is nafcillin or oxacillin (2 g IV every 4 hours). Note: Predisposing factors include stones in Stensen’s duct and dehydration. Therapy depends on identifying the specific etiologic organism. 17. For diabetic foot ulcers with <2 cm of superficial inflammation: The preferred regimen includes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (800/160 mg, 1–2 tablets orally BID) or minocycline (100 mg orally BID) combined with penicillin V potassium (500 mg orally QID) or selected cephalosporins (e.g., cefprozil, cefuroxime axetil, cefdinir, cefpodoxime) or fluoroquinolones (e.g., levofloxacin). 18. For recurrent cellulitis with chronic lymphedema prophylaxis: The preferred regimen is clindamycin (150 mg orally QD) or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (800/160 mg, 1 tablet orally QD). Alternatively, use stand-by therapy with penicillin V or amoxicillin (500–750 mg orally BID) at the onset of symptoms. 19. For methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus epidermidis: Preferred regimens include oxacillin (1–2 g IV every 4 hours), nafcillin (1–2 g IV every 4 hours), or cephalothin. Alternative regimens include rifampin (600 mg/day orally) combined with sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim or fluoroquinolones and daptomycin (600 mg orally/IV every 12 hours). Note: 75% of Staphylococcus epidermidis strains are methicillin-resistant. 20. For methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis: The preferred regimen is vancomycin (1 g IV every 12 hours) with or without rifampin (600 mg/day orally). Note: For deep-seated infections, consider adding gentamicin and/or rifampin to the regimen. 21. For prosthetic device infections: The preferred regimen is oxacillin (1–2 g IV every 4 hours) or vancomycin (1 g IV every 12 hours) combined with rifampin (600 mg/day orally) and gentamicin (3 mg/kg/day IV/IM every 8–24 hours). Note: Duration of therapy depends on the site and severity of the infection. 22. For actinomycosis: The preferred regimen is penicillin (3–4 million units IV every 4 hours for 2–6 weeks), followed by penicillin V (2–4 g/day orally QID) for 6–12 months. Alternative regimens include erythromycin, tetracycline, doxycycline, clindamycin, or minocycline. 23. For sparganosis (Spirometra mansonoides): The preferred treatment is surgical resection or ethanol injection of subcutaneous masses. Note: Praziquantel (75 mg/kg/day orally for 3 days) is controversial, as it has been ineffective in some cases but may be considered when surgery is not an option. 24. For lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, Brugia timori): The preferred regimen is diethylcarbamazine (6 mg/day orally for 12 days) with or without albendazole (400 mg orally QD). An alternative regimen is doxycycline (200 mg/day for 4 weeks) with or without ivermectin (150 μg/kg single dose). Note: Avoid ivermectin in areas where Loa loa is co-endemic due to the risk of serious adverse effects. Avoid diethylcarbamazine in certain cases.
